title: Jesse Plemons on the ‘Honor’ of Playing Plutarch in ‘The Hunger Games’ After Philip Seymour Hoffman and Debating Director Francis Lawrence Over the Character’s Motivations
description: “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” might be Haymitch Abernathy’s prequel movie, but Oscar nominee Jesse Plemons was the first person cast in
body:
“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” might be Haymitch Abernathy’s prequel movie, but Oscar nominee Jesse Plemons was the first person cast in the film.

	Plemons plays Plutarch Heavensbee, a Capitol insider, who becomes a key figure in the rebellion that sparks in the latter half of Suzanne Collins’ original trilogy of dystopian novels. In the second book, “Catching Fire,” and its 2013 film adaptation, Plutarch is introduced as the Head Gamemaker, tasked with creating the brutal trials in the Hunger Games. (The late Philip Seymour Hoffman originated the role.) At the end of that story, Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) learns that Plutarch was really scheming from inside the establishment to help support the rebels.
	

	But “Sunrise on the Reaping” takes place 25 years before those events, so casting the younger Plutarch was key.

	“I’m a huge fan of Jesse’s,” franchise director Francis Lawrence tells Variety. “Had never worked with him before, and had always wanted to, and thought he would be perfect.”

	Plemons, of course, is one of the blockbuster movie’s most accomplished stars — one of the star-studded ensemble’s seven Oscar nominees: Jennifer Lawrence and Kieran Culkin are winners, with Glenn Close receiving an honorary Oscar earlier this month.

	“We had a lot of fun casting all these people fans are familiar with for this movie. But with [Plutarch] specifically, there was a lot more development,” Lawrence adds, sharing that he and “Hunger Games” producer Nina Jacobson spent considerable time working with Collins on Plutarch’s arc.
	

	“He’s an infiltrator,” Lawrence explains. “He’s the guy at the beginning of the formation of the resistance, and at the same time, has to get to the place where by ‘Catching Fire’ he’s at Snow’s side and so trusted. So, it was on us to figure out how to portray Plutarch in a way that is believable. And that was fun because we were adding scenes that weren’t in the book.”



	

					Francis Lawrence directs Jesse Plemons in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”
									Murray Close/Lionsgate
	





	

					Philip Seymour Hoffman and Woody Harrelson in the 2013 “Hunger Games: Catching Fire”
									Murray Close/Lionsgate
	



	Book readers might’ve noticed a new Plutarch scene in the “Sunrise on the Reaping” movie — where Plemons appears bruised and bloodied after being brutally interrogated by President Snow (Ralph Fiennes), who’s learned of a secret plot to sabotage the 50th Hunger Games.

	“That was a keystone scene for us, and we went over and over and over different approaches of it,” Lawrence says. “How can we have him be active on these two distinct paths: one is, ‘How can I keep this resistance alive, but a secret?’ And ‘How can I seem utterly loyal and faithful to Snow, who is very, very smart?’ It’s become one of my favorite scenes in the movie.”

	Lawrence kicked off conversations with Plemons by sending Collins’ unpublished manuscript. The actor cracked open the book, but because he was also working on “Digger,” he hadn’t made it to the final pages before the finished script came in.

	“I read the script, and then finished the book, and was surprised by how engaging it was and how complex the character was,” Plemons tells Variety over the phone from his home in Texas. “And I was really blown away by the script and the book.”

	Indeed, Plutarch is a meaty character. But he also had to consider that the role was originated by Hoffman, one of his favorite actors of all time, who’d also played his father in 2012’s “The Master.” As such, Plemons knew saying yes would come with plenty of questions from reporters about how it felt to continue the late Hoffman’s “legacy” after the actor’s unexpected death in 2014. Even after filming the part, Plemons hasn’t quite ironed out how to articulate his feelings on such a lofty question.

	“That’s a tough one to answer,” Plemons replies, thoughtfully, when I ask how he feels about all of that. “I’m definitely honored to have the opportunity to play this character. I wish I had a better answer for you, but it’s complicated.”
	

	Less complicated are his feelings about the “Hunger Games” franchise’s larger message, which was a key factor in his decision to take the part.

	“I find it a big accomplishment when a film or a book that has such a wide appeal is able to tackle real-world themes and issues everyone feels and relates to, that connect to all of our lives,” Plemons says.

	Read on as Plemons explains how he approached Plutarch’s prequel arc, including what he garnered from Hoffman’s performance, and why he and Lawrence debated over the complex character’s true motivations.

	
		In the original trilogy, we find out that Plutarch is secretly a revolutionary. And in this story, we realize he’s had to play this role for 25 years. What struck you about that?	

	Many things. One, just the nature of doing a prequel like this. It was interesting knowing where the character ends up and how all these relationships progress, and then realizing there was actually more space to play and create ourselves. To fill in this very large blank over the course of 25 years. And there was something, just in the scope of the amount of time that he has been fighting and infiltrating the capital, there’s a sort of double agent aspect.

	There’s a sort of philosopher side to him. There’s most definitely an importance on knowledge that he’s trying to instill in Haymitch. And at the same time, what I was most interested in was his very pragmatic sense of hope, which is not at all shrouded in any sort of rose-colored idealism. It’s very rooted in the reality of how difficult and almost impossible it’s going to be, and I was just really intrigued by that on a personal level.

	The other interesting aspect is that he winds up being with the good guys, the resistance. But even still, in his relationship with Haymitch, I feel like I was constantly questioning — and I feel like the audience probably will too — just how expendable he feels Haymitch is for the greater good. All the while, he’s at least, to me, growing pretty fond of him as the story goes on. So there were just a lot of complexities that I really enjoyed.




	

					Jesse Plemons (as Plutarch Heavensbee), Joseph Zada (as Haymitch Abernathy) and Glenn Close (as Drusill Sickle) in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”
									Murray Close/Lionsgate
	



	
		One of Plutarch’s main functions is helping feed the propaganda machine. During the Reaping, for example, we see how Plutarch recognizes the bigger picture of how to tell a great story. It’s kind of cool to watch him as a director and producer, and he brings a bit of levity, too, to a very tough scene.	

	That was the first sequence I shot, which was great. It’s obvious he’s incredibly intelligent. He’s able to sort of play this role. And I really loved that sequence with Glenn [Close]. I’m assuming they’ve known each other practically all of Plutarch’s life; she’s probably like a crazy aunt in some way. And it was really fun to play with maniuplating Drusilla without her knowing it.

	It’s interesting. Obviously, his agenda is to prove himself to Snow and everyone in the Capitol. And at the same time, there must be something kind of alluring about pulling this [rebellion] off. It was really interesting, and Francis definitely allowed for some space, especially in the sequence where we’re filming Haymitch saying goodbye. We brought in a little more of the book there and a little more of Plutarch handling the camera operator, being a little more hands-on than was in the scene.


	
		Francis is known for adding scenes that are missing from the books. In this case, he expanded the scene after Snow interrogates Plutarch. Tell me a little bit about adding that scene, and what it shows about what that character endured to keep up this ruse.	

	That scene, because it was a new addition that wasn’t in the book, was something that I could definitely see the need for — to see where Plutarch was in all of this. Aside from seeing in the library earlier on, it’s the only time you get to see Plutarch with Snow, and it was just an absolute thrill getting to work with Ralph.

	It’s such a game of intellect between the two. Plutarch is trying to gauge how much Snow knows, whether he knows that he’s involved and who he knows is involved. At the same time, he’s trying to double down and act as if he’s truly working in the interest of the Capitol. We played around a lot with that scene.


	
		You and Francis sometimes disagreed about Plutarch’s motivations. What was your perspective on it?	

	I don’t think there’s like a black-or-white, or cut-and-dry, easy way of categorizing Plutarch or his motivations. The main debate Francis and I were in was whether or not his motivations were rooted in some sort of self-centeredness. A kind of wanting to be the hero, or just wanting to stick it to the Capitol and his family, that I’m sure, as a child, he had very conflicted feelings about.

	I felt his intentions were pure. The fact that he would like to stick it to the Capitol, that’s most definitely part of it. He’s most definitely entitled and privileged. But I think everyone’s given a choice, and at some point, Plutarch decided that knowledge is of the utmost importance, and I think, morally, he is very much on the side of what is right and he sees the injustice. I believe his intentions are pure. I just don’t know why you would make it all that time if your motivations were about your own self-interest.


	
		You’d get tired at a certain point. It wouldn’t be enough to fuel you for 25 years.	

	Yeah.



	

					Jesse Plemons (as Plutarch Heavensbee) in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”
									Murray Close/Lionsgate
	



	
		You had the unique circumstance of having worked with Philip Seymour Hoffman. How did you approach creating the prequel version of Plutarch? Did you watch his performance in the earlier films? Or did you call on things you observed from working together?	

	I had a lot of conversations with some of the other actors that were playing characters that were established in the other films, and we all had our own unique challenges and thoughts about how best to capture that essence, while at the same time taking some freedom in the fact that 24-25 years is a long time. The thing that jumped out at me in the film that he was in [Hoffman first appeared in 2013’s “Catching Fire”] was that they were still most definitely fully committed to the cause, but you could see the time. You could see the weariness of all those characters.

	There were little things that I was conscious of and tried to connect to his performance, but for the most part, I felt like this is a very different Plutarch. He’s beginning his journey and is incredibly ambitious, and the whole energy of his pursuit just felt very different, and all the relationships, like his relationship with Snow, are just beginning. So, it wound up feeling like there was quite a bit of room.


	
		The whole idea is Suzanne writes the book, and that determines where there’ll be more movies. But because there is so much more of Plutarch’s story to potentially tell, would you be interested in signing on again if that opportunity came?	

	Most definitely. I can’t imagine where her mind will go next — no one can. But, personally, selfishly, what I would love to see is Plutarch’s teenage years. I thought a lot about that while we were shooting, but I don’t think I could play that part.
	
		I don’t know. There are prosthetic ways or de-aging ways we could make this happen.	

	[Laughs.] Like “The Irishman.” 


	This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.

schema.headline: Jesse Plemons on the ‘Honor’ of Playing Plutarch in ‘The Hunger Games’ After Philip Seymour Hoffman and Debating Director Francis Lawrence Over the Character’s Motivations

title: Asha Bhosle and S. Janaki Remembered by Singer K.S. Chithra and Suhasini Maniratnam at IFFI’s Lata Mangeshkar Talk
description: Asha Bhosle and S. Janaki, two of Indian cinema’s most celebrated playback singers, were remembered at the 57th International Film Festival of Indi
body:
Asha Bhosle and S. Janaki, two of Indian cinema’s most celebrated playback singers, were remembered at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa by singer K.S. Chithra and actor-filmmaker Suhasini Maniratnam.

	Bhosle, a two-time Grammy nominee whose name was referenced in Cornershop’s 1997 hit “Brimful of Asha,” died in April at 92. Janaki, known as the Nightingale of South India, died in July at 88. Chithra and Suhasini shared their memories of the two at the annual “Lata Mangeshkar Talk: The Voice That Echoes Forever,” named for Bhosle’s elder sister, the singer Lata Mangeshkar.
	

	Chithra, who has recorded more than 25,000 songs in several Indian languages over a career spanning nearly five decades, spoke about the singers who shaped her musical sensibilities, among them Mangeshkar, P. Susheela and Janaki. She imitated Janaki as a child, while acknowledging that the veteran singer’s distinctive style was impossible to reproduce. Mangeshkar’s devotional songs, she said, had particularly impressed her with their emotional depth.

	Suhasini recalled an episode from the making of “Iruvar” (1997), directed by her husband Mani Ratnam. Composer A.R. Rahman, an Oscar winner for “Slumdog Millionaire,” had invited Bhosle to record a song that needed to evoke the style of Tamil playback singer L.R. Eswari, but was unsure how to explain the reference to her. He asked Suhasini to help. She demonstrated Eswari’s style, and Bhosle went on to deliver “Venilla Venilla.”

	Chithra spoke about Bhosle’s versatility and her ability to move between musical forms, including ghazals, and about her desire to establish her own musical identity rather than be compared with her sister. At their first meeting, Chithra said, Bhosle asked her why she was singing in such a high register.
	

	Janaki, Suhasini said, could inhabit a character through her voice, singing like a child or a teenage boy. Chithra recalled that Janaki was a devoted fan of Mangeshkar. She would play Mangeshkar’s songs on the radio, turn down the volume during the vocal portions and record herself singing along – “like a karaoke on her own,” as Chithra described it. Offstage, Chithra said, Janaki would feed her by hand when she visited her home.

	The session also touched on the demands of recording and on recognizing one’s vocal limitations with age.

	Chithra sang snippets throughout, including songs from her own repertoire and numbers popularized by Janaki and Bhosle. In a closing quiz, film clips were played without their background scores and Chithra was asked to identify each song by singing it. She identified all five.

	The session ended with Chithra singing “Paadariyen” from “Sindhu Bhairavi” (1985), which won her the first of her six National Film Awards, as Suhasini, who starred in the film, joined her, lip-syncing.

title: Gerald R. Molen, Oscar-Winning ‘Schindler’s List’ Producer, Dies at 91
description:
Gerald R. Molen, the Oscar-winning producer behind Steven Spielberg’s “Schindler’s List,” has died. He was 91.

	Molen’s death was announced by his
body:
Gerald R. Molen, the Oscar-winning producer behind Steven Spielberg’s “Schindler’s List,” has died. He was 91.

	Molen’s death was announced by his great-niece, Rachel Lorraine Pullan, in an Instagram post on Sunday.

	“This morning my great-uncle, Gerald R. Molen, passed on to join my great-grandma and his dear wife Pat on the other side of the veil. I am so happy for him, and also so very sad,” she wrote. “Uncle Jerry was a man of great moral character and high integrity. He started doing work, moving set pieces and driving at a movie studio and worked his way up to the position of producer.”
	

	Molen frequently collaborated with Spielberg throughout his career. He served as producer on “Jurassic Park,” “Minority Report,” “Hook” and “The Lost World: Jurassic Park,” as well as “Schindler’s List,” which won best picture in 1994. Molen shared the Oscar with Spielberg and Branko Lustig. Molen also worked on several Amblin Entertainment films, such as “The Flintstones,” “The Little Rascals,” “Little Giants,” “Casper” and “Twister.”

	Molen’s working relationship with Spielberg began in 1985 when he worked as a unit production manager on “The Color Purple.” That job led to an associate producer role on 1987’s “*batteries not included,” on which Spielberg served as executive producer.

	Molen’s other producer credits include “Rain Man,” “Days of Thunder,” “Just Like Heaven,” “The Meg,” “Meg 2” and “The Best Christmas Pageant Ever.”

	Born in Montana in 1935, Molen moved to North Hollywood in 1947. His parents, Gerald Sr. and Edith, owned and operated a cafe next to the Republic Pictures lot in Studio City.
	

	Molen’s wife of almost 70 years, Pat, died in January 2024 at 86 years old.

title: ‘Blade Runner 2099’ Boss Silka Luisa on What the Finale Means for Replicants and the Fate of Cora and Olwen
description:
Nov 26, 2026 5:00pm PT	
	

	
		‘Blade Runner 2099’ Boss Silka Luisa on What the Finale Means for Replicants and the Fate of Cora and
body:
Nov 26, 2026 5:00pm PT	
	

	
		‘Blade Runner 2099’ Boss Silka Luisa on What the Finale Means for Replicants and the Fate of Cora and Olwen
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Courtesy of Clay Enos/Prime Video
	

		
	
				

	SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for the finale of “Blade Runner 2099,” now streaming on Prime Video.

	In the finale of “Blade Runner 2099,” the future of humanity is anything but certain. 

	After discovering that the stolen memory they’ve spent the series searching for contains Dr. Eldon Tyrell’s (Joe Turkell) original Nexus-1 replicant design, Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) and Cora (Hunter Schafer) face off against Julius (Sam C. Wilson), whose plans to create a new generation of replicants threaten to reshape the future of both humans and replicants.
	

	Olwen ultimately kills Julius, but not before he destroys the memory containing the secrets to his original design. In a final twist, Olwen, who was living out the last few days of her pre-determined lifespan as a replicant, discovers she has been transformed into a Nexus-1 herself and can now live the longer life she wished for. Meanwhile, Cora learns that Helena (Sheila Atim), the woman who raised her and Elias (Lewis Gribben), was a replicant, forcing her to reconsider everything she previously believed about humanity and explore the possibility that humans and replicants aren’t so different after all.



	

					Left to right: Elias (Lewis Gribben), Cora (Hunter Schafer), and Bebeto (Dimitri Abold) 
									Courtesy of Clay Enos/Prime Video
	



	Elias, on the other hand, a more radical approach. Determined to fight back against the replicants and reclaim societal control as humans, he broadcasts a message to the population of Los Angeles falsely claiming responsibility for destroying the replicant birthing center in hopes of sparking a human uprising (Julius was the one responsible). But there is no rebellion. The replicants are still in control, and Elias’ fate is unknown.
	

	Cora returns the LAPD, where she undergoes another Index test overseen by Greta (Katelyn Rose Downey) — a parallel to the premiere episode in which the results revealed she possesses no empathy, despite being a human. This time, however, Cora has developed empathy after learning to care for Olwen, who is now jetting off-world.

	Below, “Blade Runner 2099” creator Silka Luisa breaks down the finale and what it means for the future of replicants in the “Blade Runner” universe.

	
		I should start by telling you that I’m one of the select few who haven’t seen any of the “Blade Runner” films.	

	Oh my gosh! What did you think? I’m so curious. What did you understand? What didn’t you understand?


	
		I loved it! The replicants are so intelligent and advanced that it took me a second to figure out who was actually human.	

	Exactly. We had a lot of conversations about, “Should we change their costume? Should we make it clear who is what?” But what makes the world so unsettling is that you never really know, and I love that about the films. It was really important to us that you were never really on firm ground there.



	

					Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer
									Courtesy of Clay Enos/Prime Video
	




	
		That’s part of what made it so fun. This series was such a great introduction to the “Blade Runner” world.	

	That’s so gratifying, because so many early conversations were had about how we make this accessible for people that haven’t seen one of the films, both of the films or read the book. We had to find an entry point with original characters that you’re also not going to have to catch everybody up to a bunch of lore.


	
		And I loved the ending. So that means the replicants are still in control?	

	Yeah. Sorry. At the end of the day, it’s noir. It’s not a revolution story, and that’s why it was so important with the Elias storyline to give this sense of, “Is there going to be a rebellion? Is there going to be an uprising?” No. It’s really just capitalism, and you’re in a noir world where no one is coming to save you. This is the status quo, and you have to carve out your own future within these new circumstances.


	
		Elias was so intent on starting this revolution for humans to be back in control. What was your approach to creating that storyline for him?	

	Elias’ story is about someone who is really just trying to find agency. At the beginning of the season, he’s taken care of by his sister, which is beautiful, but is very claustrophobic. And then he thinks that there’s going to be some kind of uprising, and they’re going to be able to recreate the world that once was. The truth is that that’s not what’s going to happen, and there’s no one coming to save the day for him. While that is deflating, it’s also an opportunity for him to falsely claim that he did this act of terrorism, because the truth is, if you want change in the world, sometimes you have to be the spark that ignites it. And it was really just trying to find a moment in the sun for him too, so that he could really be the change or be the hope for change that he wanted.



	

									Courtesy of Clay Enos/Prime Video
	




	
		After he hacks the intercom, the next thing we see is Cora taking the Index test. Will we ever get to find out what happened to Elias? Or was than something you wanted to keep open to interpretation?	

	It’s the same as with “[Blade Runner] 2049,” where I was like, “I think this is what happens four months later.” I’m sure everyone had different ideas. I obviously have my own story for each character and how I imagine it will continue, but there’s definitely a reason we cut the rope at the points we did.


	
		I do want to talk about Cora taking the Index test with Greta. Was that based on the empathy test from the original 1982 movie?	

	That test has been an evolution through the films. In the first film, there’s a void comp test, which is a straight up empathy test to tell the difference between replicant and human. In “2049,” there’s a baseline test, which measures emotional stability to see if you’re able to be a police officer.

	We’ve blended those, because now that replicants are policing the human population, there’s a risk that they could develop empathy. If they develop empathy, it makes it harder to put intubating bags over them and police them, and you don’t want that.


	
		The second time Cora takes the test, she gets different results.	

	It was an important mirror scene to the end of the pilot, where she essentially passes that test, meaning she doesn’t have any empathy. So she is a human who’s just been stripped of her humanity, and I think that if empathy is the distinction between replicant and human, it’s so interesting, because it is not definitive. It’s something that you can gain or lose. 

	And at the beginning of this series, she lost it. Then at the end through this connection with Olwen, she rediscovers it.



	

									Courtesy of Clay Enos/Prime Video
	




	
		Cora and Olwen’s relationship grew so much. Just before Olwen kills Julius, she’s holding Cora in an almost maternal way.	

	Yeah. I think Cora has lost her own mother figure in Helena, and the surprise of the season for her is that she finds the surrogate mother in Olwen at the end.


	
		The final shot of the series is Olwen flying off-world. Did you always know you wanted to end with that?	

	I knew we wanted to end on a glimpse of off-world, which, if you’re a fan, has been very mythologized. We wanted to give a little peek of what it could be, but trying to find some hope in the ending.


	
		It felt very human for Olwen — returning to the place where she was the happiest.	

	Exactly. And the endings of the films are ambiguous. They don’t give you definitive answers, and there’s been a lot of debate about both of them, even in the writers’ room, about how we all understood certain final moments, which is always so much fun because I think that it just shows you that everyone is having an engaged and personal experience of the material. That was really what we were trying to strike that balance: how do we make this feel conclusive enough so that people know we have given them a true ending, but at the same time honor the films and leave enough questions for people to debate?


	
		This wasn’t necessarily an ambiguous ending, but I did wish Olwen could get some closure from Malik (Noah Ritter).	

	It’s a tragedy, in this sense where they never get to have a forever ever together. She tells Cora to shoot on sight, and she does. And I think that she doesn’t really believe him when he’s saying why he left her. I wanted her storyline and her romance to actually be a very human romance. She’s really a wounded lover who’s been left in her final days, and she doesn’t understand why. And the real emotional reason she’s searching for answers is, she wants to understand why she was abandoned.


	
		Tell me about the memory of the Nexus-1 design. What does that mean for replicants?	

	In the lore, they don’t give you a lot of details about what Tyrell’s original intentions were and the original different models. That always seemed intentional. So, when you think about Tyrell as a character, he’s so grand in the first film, and he’s such a dreamer. He seems so poetic. It just doesn’t seem like he would have created these beings to be something small and just for labor, and that never really made sense to me from who he was. Those two things didn’t seem like they fit, and so I was thinking, “What was his original intention when he made replicants?” He seems to have such a God complex. He would really want to create what comes next, the “next us.” And that is something that is better than us. It’s not smaller. It doesn’t have smaller lifespans. It’s meant to go further. It’s meant to extend far beyond.


	
		And we’ve never gotten to see a world where replicants are in control before.	

	No. The end of “2049” gives you the sense that there is a possibility of a mutiny brewing, and my own mind as an audience member was just like, “Oh, well, they’re going to uprise.” That’s what I assumed happened, and so that was how I filled in the gap personally. And this is really just in the aftermath of what that would look like.


	
		It’s scary, because this feels so plausible in the world we’re in now. This could happen if we’re not careful.	

	It’s been part of the conversation for a couple years now, and I think it’s obviously coming to a head with all of the AI debate, because we really are having a mirror held up to us, and we’re starting to ask, “What is the value of humans? What can we do that nothing else can do? What is our purpose if we don’t work right?” All these big philosophical questions are being forced upon us, so it’s a really intense moment to be alive. Growing up, I never had this fear that humanity could ever end. That there would be a passing of the baton to something else, and it’s been in the zeitgeist. That was definitely in my mind as I started the project.



	

									Courtesy of Clay Enos/Prime Video
	




	
		The two “Blade Runner” films were led by Harrison Ford and Ryan Gosling. What made you want to explore this world through a female perspective?	

	If you’re going to ask the question of, “What does it mean to be human?,” it does make sense to want to have more points of view on that, and that definitely felt like an addition to the conversation.


	
		I also have to ask about one of my favorite scenes, which is when they went to the Body Body Shop. There were vending machines with prosthetic pregnant bellies and aged body parts that replicants could purchase to live out these uniquely human experiences. How did you come up with that idea?	

	That was probably one of my favorite sets and sequences in the series. I just love the idea that, even though replicants have power, they still have this longing for what they can’t have. It was so fun to build that out. We looked at a lot of real-world references from ’70s New York and real peep shows, and the coin is taken from the real slots that they would have. There’s so many fun details in world building. You have this concept which is just prosthetics. How would you have that? How would you actually try and assimilate that in this kind of grungy underworld? The idea that you never get to grow old with someone is when Olwen emotionally realizes that her life has been cut so short.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.



	
		More from Variety

schema.headline: ‘Blade Runner 2099’ Boss Silka Luisa on What the Finale Means for Replicants and the Fate of Cora and Olwen

title: Chiwetel Ejiofor on How Stephen Frears’ ‘Dirty Pretty Things’ Led Him to Fall in Love With Film
description: Chiwetel Ejiofor started his film career by doing something that many would consider as the absolute peak: he made a film with Steven Spielberg.
body:
Chiwetel Ejiofor started his film career by doing something that many would consider as the absolute peak: he made a film with Steven Spielberg.

	“Amistad” was his very first film and, understandably, he was afraid of peaking too soon.

	“I was definitely worried about it at the time,” he said at Torino Film Festival.


	“You feel that there are stages to how you develop as an actor and the opportunities you get, and you think they might follow a very linear path. But of course, my first film role was with Steven Spielberg. I realized then, very early on, that it’s a deeply unpredictable profession. You can either feel disquiet or anxiety about that, or you have to go with it.”
	

	He added: “The opportunities can be sporadic or come from different places and angles that you didn’t imagine. Part of the challenge, but also the exciting thing about being an actor, is having the capacity and ability to roll with it, to travel on the journey of it and see where it takes you.”

	The British actor came to Italy to receive the Stella della Mole award for lifetime achievement.

	He admitted that, for the longest time, he didn’t see himself as a film actor.

	“Even though I had done the Steven Spielberg film, I still thought of myself primarily as a theater actor. I worked with the National Theatre in Great Britain, in the West End and with many off-West End theater companies,” he said. In 2008, he won the Laurence Olivier Award for best actor for “Othello.”

	It took Stephen Frears’ thriller “Dirty Pretty Things” – which screened at Torino Film Festival on Thursday – to finally change his mind. Frears also received an award at the festival this week. 
	

	“I think it was around that time when I started to fall in love with film as well, with film acting and the rhythm and poetry of cinema. A lot of that had to do with Stephen Frears and Chris Menges, who was the cinematographer on that film. It became something that I started to pursue.”

	For a while, he was able to “balance the two very well.”

	“It was when I became more involved in writing and directing that it started taking up a lot of my time outside of acting in films. Historically, this would have been the time I spent on stage. I ended up writing or directing my own films.”

	Ejiofor has directed two feature films: “Rob Peace” and “The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind.” But his return to theater is imminent.

	“It’s still something that I’m very passionate about. Finding the time to do as much theater as I want can be challenging, but it’s something I’m in the midst of conversations about.”

	He hopes to be involved in another theater production later on next year. In the meantime, he’s happy to reflect on some of the highlights of his career, which includes Oscar-winning “12 Years a Slave,” directed by Steve McQueen, also shown at the Italian fest.

	In the film, he played Solomon Northup, a free black man who was kidnapped in 1841 and sold into slavery in Louisiana. 

	“I hadn’t heard of his story at all. When I was sent the script, I was incredibly moved and shocked by it. Then I read Northup’s own memoir. I thought it was an extraordinary story, an extraordinary tale,” he said before the screening, praising the story that captured a “very tragic period of absence of humanity.”

	“It felt very profound to me. I was just deeply moved. Steve McQueen is a phenomenal filmmaker, incredibly passionate, detailed and thorough, with a wonderful vision and cinematic heart. It was incredibly gratifying to see the film being received the way that it was, globally and by the Academy.”

	He noted: “At its heart, it was always a story about human respect and human dignity.”

schema.headline: Chiwetel Ejiofor on How Stephen Frears’ ‘Dirty Pretty Things’ Led Him to Fall in Love With Film

title: John Travolta Didn’t Recognize Himself as Alleged JFK Assassin Johnny Roselli in ‘November 1963’: ‘I Went, “Oh My God, He’s the Devil”’
description:
John Travolta rarely connects with all his characters. Sometimes, he even loves to hate them. 

	“They say you have to find something you like,” th
body:
John Travolta rarely connects with all his characters. Sometimes, he even loves to hate them. 

	“They say you have to find something you like,” the actor explains. “But I’ve never felt that. I think you have to like the result, pulling it off. That’s where the joy comes from. To become these people, you don’t have to identify with them or enjoy being them. You just have to be excellent at executing them.” 


	Even so, Travolta faced one of the biggest challenges of his career playing a rather literal executioner in Roland Joffé’s “November 1963,” which opened the Torino Film Festival with its international premiere. 
	

	On paper, Johnny Roselli seems right in Travolta’s wheelhouse: a real-life wiseguy turned showbiz fixer, an Al Capone protégé whose career took him from Hollywood to Las Vegas to the Bay of Pigs, leaving a trail of bodies along the way. 

	“He was an odd mix,” says Travolta. “He was the guy who asked Sinatra to connect Kennedy with the mob. He hooked Kennedy up with Marilyn Monroe. He was a Hollywood icon of sorts, and had this other, darker side as a hitman. That’s complex. I’ve done dark subject matter before, but this was real. It actually happened, and that’s the difference.”

	Roselli was purportedly a CIA go-between and sharpshooter. “November 1963” takes that history a step further, imagining him as a key triggerman on the Grassy Knoll, directly responsible for the killing that shook a nine-year-old boy in Englewood, New Jersey, and still haunts the actor to this day. 

	“It was the biggest crime of the century,” says Travolta, instantly transported back to second grade. “The announcement came at 11 a.m. Eastern Standard Time that the President had been shot, and then three hours later, at 2 p.m., they confirmed that he had passed. We all went to our homes, and all I can remember is being home with my father, glued to the television, sitting on his lap and trying to make sense of it all.”
	

	Travolta carried that weight onto the set, where, he says, he was asked “to play a very evil man with moments of humanity.” 

	“The actors were all suffering because everybody who was hired was a very decent person, and we all had to play, to some degree, people who were not,” he continues. “So it was harder to go home every night. It took a glass of wine and a nice dinner to snap out of the zone.” 

	That feeling returned in full force when Travolta finally watched his finished performance at Torino’s opening night, prompting a kind of out-of-body experience.

	 “I thought, ‘Wow, I can’t believe that’s me,’” he says. “I’ve never seen myself lose my soul in a film, and [here] I was soulless. I was very proud that I could portray that, because it’s against my very essence. When I looked at it on screen, I went, ‘Oh my god, he’s the devil.’” 

	Written and produced by family members of Windy City crime boss Sam Giancana, “November 1963” foregrounds the Chicago Outfit’s role in the assassination plot, leaving CIA and government involvement for a possible follow-up. 

	“This is not history; it’s about human beings,” Travolta says. “There will be lots more to tell, but you can’t do it all at the same time.” 

	That deliberately incomplete picture appealed to Joffé, who translates the murky history into a mise-en-scène of skewed angles and funhouse reflections. 

	“That’s how history comes to us,” he says. “I’d say this story is probably 90% true, insofar as no one will ever know what really happened. What’s most important to me is whether it’s credible. And has that mindset changed? The transactional mindset, the mafia mindset, the idea that power is all that counts and loyalty has to be bought at the point of a gun. My feeling is that it doesn’t disappear. It transmutes. It may become a political party. It may become the way business acts.” 

	In one telling revision, the film casts slain Dallas policeman J.D. Tippit, whose murder was attributed to Lee Harvey Oswald, as a key conspirator. Joffé uses the twist to further muddy the waters while dismissing the notion of a neatly orchestrated plot. 

	“I reject the conspiracy theory,” he says. “If it were a conspiracy, we would have known by now, and we absolutely do not. What it was is collusion, and collusion is very different. Collusion is subtle. It happens in the shadows. It’s a nod, a wink, a knowing glance. It’s putting a gun in the right place.” 
	

	The distinction, he argues, is that no grand design is required. The CIA and organized crime had already worked together on plots to kill Fidel Castro, but that didn’t mean anyone had to convene a committee to plan Kennedy’s assassination. 

	“It’s not about control,” Joffé says. “It’s about the fact that life is chaotic, and the killing of the President comes out of that. We made a film about chaos.”

title: Luca Guadagnino Wants Next Movie to Be a ‘Love Story,’ Confirms ‘American Psycho’ and ‘Separate Rooms’ Not Happening
description:
Luca Guadagnino wants to return to romance.

	Speaking to Variety at the Marrakech Film Festival where he’s presenting “Artificial,” the Italian fi
body:
Luca Guadagnino wants to return to romance.

	Speaking to Variety at the Marrakech Film Festival where he’s presenting “Artificial,” the Italian filmmaker behind “Call Me by Your Name,” “Bones and All” and “Queer” revealed that he hopes his next directorial endeavor will be another love story.

	“I think a lot of inspiration could come from facts of history,” Guadagnino said when asked what he would like to explore in his next film. “I want to make another love story, so I have to think about it, but I want to make a kind movie, another love story.”
	

“I want to make another love story, a kind movie,” Luca Guadagnino said at #MarrakechFilmFestival.However, the Italian director confirmed that the queer romance “Separate Rooms,” originally set to star Josh O’Connor, is no longer in the works.  Guadagnino also addressed the… pic.twitter.com/kTmz3PlAZr— Variety (@Variety) November 26, 2026


	He also confirmed that two of his previously announced projects — a new adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’ “American Psycho” and the gay romance “Separate Rooms” — are no longer moving forward with him.

	“Separate Rooms” was set to be an adaptation of Italian writer Pier Vittorio Tondelli’s 1989 novel about a writer grappling with the death of his lover. Josh O’Connor, who previously worked with Guadagnino on “Challengers,” and Léa Seydoux had been linked to the project since 2024.

	“I don’t think I’m doing a movie with Léa Seydoux, unfortunately. That’s not happening,” Guadagnino said. “But I would love to work with Léa, of course.”

	The director also addressed the demise of his “American Psycho” adaptation, which was first announced by Lionsgate in October 2024. The film, penned by Scott Z. Burns, was intended to be a fresh interpretation of Ellis’ 1991 novel rather than a remake of Mary Harron’s 2000 cult classic starring Christian Bale. “That’s the job of a director,” he said of its dissolution. “You direct movies and sometimes it happens, sometimes it doesn’t. It’s very simple and linear and usual.”
	

	The filmmaker also dispelled speculation that Robert Pattinson had been in contention to play Patrick Bateman, though he said “he’s a perfect choice for James Bond,” adding: “He’s an incredible star, he’s done so many great roles and I wish someday to work with him, of course.”

	Would Guadagnino direct a Bond film? “I would say yes, yes, of course,” he said of the prospect. “I would like to play with icons.”

	The director’s upcoming film, “Artificial,” marks another departure from the sweeping romances that have come to define much of his oeuvre. The Amazon MGM Studios feature dramatizes the turmoil at OpenAI surrounding the ousting and subsequent reinstatement of CEO Sam Altman, played by Andrew Garfield.

	The film premiered at New York Film Festival and screens at Marrakech Film Festival on Thursday night.

schema.headline: Luca Guadagnino Wants Next Movie to Be a ‘Love Story,’ Confirms ‘American Psycho’ and ‘Separate Rooms’ Not Happening

title: Jessy Moussallem’s ‘Faux Bijoux,’ Laila Abbas’ ‘America Is Behind the Door’ Take Top Prizes at Marrakech’s Atlas Workshops
description: Jessy Moussallem’s “Faux Bijoux” and Laila Abbas’ “America Is Behind the Door” claimed the top post-production and development prizes, respectively
body:
Jessy Moussallem’s “Faux Bijoux” and Laila Abbas’ “America Is Behind the Door” claimed the top post-production and development prizes, respectively, at this year’s Atlas Workshops, the industry strand running Nov. 22 – 26 as part of the Marrakech Film Festival.

	The winner of a post-production grant in the amount of €30,000 ($33,000), Moussallem’s debut feature is an expansion of the short film of the same name, which screened at Sundance and Clermont-Ferrand. It follows the members of a family who are caught up in debts and schemes that drag them into a vicious cycle and test their unity.
	

	With principal photography underway, the Lebanese filmmaker couldn’t attend the Atlas Workshops. In a director’s statement, she wrote: “‘Faux Bijoux’ was born from a question rooted in my family and in Lebanon: Why is truth sometimes too difficult to speak? Behind our obsession with appearances lies a struggle for dignity, and a desire to protect those we love.” She added: “The film explores how love survives unspoken truths, and how lying can become its only possible language.”

	The post-production jury of festival programmer and distributor Eddie Bertozzi (Be Water Film), filmmaker Mohamed Kordofani (“Goodbye Julia”) and artistic director Kristy Matheson (BFI Festivals) awarded the second prize of €10,000 ($11,000) to two films: “Hamlet From the Slums,” by Ahmed Fawzi-Saleh, and “Occupational Hazards,” by Bassel Ghandour.

	Following his 2018 Rotterdam premiere “Poisonous Roses,” Egyptian filmmaker Fawzi-Saleh’s sophomore feature follows Ahmed, a restless and stifled young man who lives under the strict rule of his widower father, the self-proclaimed “King of the Junkyard.” When a revelation sets off a chain of events no one can control, Ahmed is drawn into a search for the truth that will cost him everything.
	

	Jordanian writer, director and producer Ghandour wrote and produced the Academy Award-nominated film “Theeb.” His directorial debut, “The Alleys,” premiered at Locarno’s Piazza Grande. Set in Jerusalem, “Occupational Hazards” follows a Palestinian family that fights to keep their home from crumbling, both literally and figuratively, as their struggle against the system takes on wild and unorthodox forms.

	The third prize, in the amount of €10,000 ($11,000), went to “My Father Killed Bourguiba,” by Fatma Riahi. The latest from the Tunisian director, whose debut, “A Haunted Past,” premiered at IDFA in 2018, is a deeply personal journey into the story of the filmmaker’s father, who was part of a failed coup attempt against Tunisia’s first president, Habib Bourguiba.

	Development jurors Nadim Cheikhrouha (Mime Films), Marie-Ange Luciani (Les Films de Pierre) and Linda Mutawi (Fikra) awarded the top prize of €25,000 ($27,400) to the Palestinian filmmaker Abbas, whose debut “Thank You for Banking With Us!” premiered at the BFI London Film Festival in 2024.

	Her sophomore feature follows an exhausted Palestinian mother who faces a series of impossible confrontations over the course of the 10 days before her U.S. citizenship interview. The closer that fateful day comes, the less she can separate suburban life from a genocide enabled by the country of which she is about to become.

	“I am interested in what politics does to human behavior: how it changes the way people parent, argue, joke, choose silence, or decide to speak,” Abbas wrote in a director’s statement. “As a Palestinian filmmaker, I am drawn to moments when absurdity and grief occupy the same space, because that is where life feels most truthful to me.

	“At a moment when Palestine feels almost impossible to speak about outside the immediacy of catastrophe, I choose to tell this story from a distance. Setting the film in the United States gives me a wider lens through which to look back at Palestine — to hold grief and anger without being consumed by them, and to examine political and human contradictions with greater clarity,” she continued. “The film engages with the role of the United States in sustaining the destruction in Palestine, while exposing the contradiction between the country’s founding promise as a place for immigrants and the realities many immigrants encounter now.”
	

	The development jury awarded its second prize of €10,000 ($11,000) to “Waltz of the Savages,” by Yasmine Benkiran, whose first feature, “Queens,” premiered at the Venice Film Festival. The Moroccan-born filmmaker’s latest is set in the 1950s in an Arab country under French colonial rule, where the most lavish party in the nation’s history is about to be staged, while outside, rebellion brews.

	The third prize of €10,000 ($11,000) went to “Eko Gongon,” by Cabo Verde’s Carlos Yuri Ceuninck, whose last documentary, “Omi Nobu,” won the top prize at Burkina Faso’s FESPACO film festival. The film takes place in a fishing village threatened by globalization, where the Gongon — a rare endemic seabird and a phantasmagoric, shapeshifting figure from oral tradition — haunts the archipelago’s imagination.

	The fourth prize of €5,000 ($5,500) went to “Safara,” a feature debut by Senegalese filmmaker Awa Moctar Gueye, which follows the trials of a tomboyish teenager on the suffocating streets of Safara, a neighborhood whose name means “hell.” The fifth prize of €5,000 ($5,500) went to “Chronicles of an Unannounced Death,” by Syrian German writer, director and producer Dyaa Naim. It follows a Syrian undertaker living in Germany whose life and past are turned upside down when he learns his recently deceased father wanted to be buried in Damascus.

	Lastly, the Atlas Close-Ups jury, which was comprised of producer Amine Benjelloun (Ali n’ Productions) and programmer Delly Shirazi (Intl. Film Festival Rotterdam), gave a prize of €5,000 ($5,500) to “The Cemetery’s Bird,” by writer-director Madane El Ghazouani, awarding it for its “boldness, a big heart and something new as a cinematic proposal for Morocco’s national cinema.” El Ghazouani’s first feature, “Bad Weather,” won four prizes at the Marrakech Film Festival in 2025.

	Since their inception in 2018, the Atlas Workshops have supported 242 projects — including 111 Moroccan films — with 42 of those having been selected by Cannes, Venice or Berlin. Nearly half the films in this year’s main competition in Marrakech are alumni of the program, including Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo’s Cannes Camera d’Or winner “Ben’Imana” and Rafiki Fariala’s Un Certain Regard prizewinner “Congo Boy.”
	

	At Thursday’s ceremony, Marrakech festival director and Atlas Workshops founder Rémi Bonhomme celebrated the “rich program” at this year’s edition, underscoring how the participants continue to make the event “a very vibrant place for Arab and African cinema.”

	“The Atlas Workshops is a spirit. It’s a spirit that has been the same since the very first edition in 2018,” Bonhomme said. “How to define the spirit of the Workshops? I think it has a lot to do with the conviction to place the filmmaker and the creative process at the heart of everything we do. We really support the vision. We really accompany them and support them in making the boldest film as possible.

	“We live in a time when we need, more than ever, free and daring cinematic voices. We really need voices that can challenge dominant narratives,” Bonhomme added. “We need voices that can really change our perspective of the world, and I truly think that’s what we do here at the Atlas Workshops, edition after edition.”

	The Marrakech Film Festival runs through Nov. 28.

schema.headline: Jessy Moussallem’s ‘Faux Bijoux,’ Laila Abbas’ ‘America Is Behind the Door’ Take Top Prizes at Marrakech’s Atlas Workshops

title: Thanksgiving Earthquake Hits Off Baja California Coast, Magnitude 5.7
description:
Thanksgiving Shake-Up
                          5.7 Quake Strikes Off Baja Coast
body:
Thanksgiving Shake-Up
                          5.7 Quake Strikes Off Baja Coast
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              A magnitude 5.7 earthquake struck a remote group of islands off Mexico's Baja California peninsula on Thanksgiving ... delivering a holiday shake-up in the Pacific Ocean.
      
    
              The quake hit Thursday near the Revillagigedo Islands, roughly 216 miles from Cabo San Lucas, at a depth of about 6 miles.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Fortunately, the remote location means the earthquake is unlikely to affect many people ... though it's unclear whether any aftershocks could strike closer to the mainland ... and the region was already rattled by a magnitude 4.2 earthquake just one day earlier.
      

              The Revillagigedo Islands are volcanic and federally protected by Mexico, boasting such a rich marine ecosystem that National Geographic has dubbed them the "Galápagos of Mexico."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              The Thanksgiving tremor comes just days after back-to-back earthquakes shook Southern California's beach cities ... including a magnitude 3.2 quake in Orange County early Monday and a magnitude 3.3 quake off Manhattan Beach on Sunday.
      
    
              Mexico also experienced a magnitude 4.7 earthquake in Baja California earlier this month.
      
    
              For now, it appears the holiday got off to a shaky start, with no major destruction.

title: Venomous Sea Snakes Washing Ashore on Southern California Beaches, Officials Warn
description:
California Beaches
                          Venomous Snakes Washing Ashore
body:
California Beaches
                          Venomous Snakes Washing Ashore
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 26, 2026
                            5:00 PM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 26, 2026
                                5:37 PM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              California beachgoers might want to watch where they step ... 'cause venomous sea snakes are washing ashore ... and experts warn more could be on the way.
      
    
              A yellow-bellied sea snake was discovered Sunday at Bolsa Chica State Beach in Orange County ... marking just the eighth documented sighting of the rare reptile in Southern California.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              And here's the kicker ... scientists believe unusually warm waters from El Niño are pushing the tropical snakes farther north, meaning this slithery surprise might not be the last.
      

              Researchers at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County say high tides through Sunday could bring more snakes onto beaches, with additional sightings possible in early and late December .
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Despite their dangerous venom, the snakes aren't typically aggressive toward humans. Still, officials are warning beachgoers to keep their hands off ... advising anyone who spots one to snap a photo from a safe distance and alert lifeguards.
      
    
              So, if you're hitting the beach this holiday weekend ... keep your eyes on the sand ... you never know what might wash up.

title: Florida Thanksgiving Feast Leaves 18 Sick, 15 Hospitalized
description:
Florida Thanksgiving Nightmare
                          15 Hospitalized After Suspected Food Poi
body:
Florida Thanksgiving Nightmare
                          15 Hospitalized After Suspected Food Poisoning
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                November 26, 2026
                
                            3:30 PM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 26, 2026
                                4:35 PM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              A Thanksgiving feast in Florida turned into a holiday nightmare ... with 18 people falling ill from suspected food poisoning and at least 15 landing in the hospital.
      
    
              The dinner disaster unfolded Wednesday at Leon Medical Centers' headquarters in Doral, near Miami, where employees gathered for an early Thanksgiving celebration.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              But the holiday cheer didn't last long ... several staffers began experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms after the catered meal, prompting a massive emergency response.
      

              According to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, 18 people reported feeling sick, with 15 initially transported to hospitals. The situation was serious enough for officials to declare a Level 3 mass casualty incident.
      
    
              Leon Medical Centers confirmed an outside catering company provided the food and says it's working to determine what went wrong ... stressing that no patients were affected.
      
    
              Safe to say ... nobody's asking for seconds.

title: Tom Hardy Back Filming 'MobLand' Season 3 After Rumors He Was Fired
description:
Tom Hardy
                          I'm Not Sleeping With the Fishes ...
body:
Tom Hardy
                          I'm Not Sleeping With the Fishes ...
                          Back on 'MobLand' Set
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Tom Hardy is back in the mob business ... and after months of behind-the-scenes drama threatening his future on "MobLand," the actor has finally been spotted back on set.
      
    
              The "Venom" star was photographed filming Season 3 of the Paramount+ crime series in London Tuesday, appearing to be in good spirits as he laughed and joked with crew members.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              It's the first time Hardy has been photographed filming since reports surfaced earlier this year that he'd been fired following alleged clashes with producers.
      

              As TMZ previously reported ... Hardy was accused of hiding out in his trailer for hours, keeping co-stars Helen Mirren and Pierce Brosnan waiting, and butting heads with producers over scripts and dialogue.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              However, TMZ confirmed in June that Hardy would return for Season 3 after a meeting in London with producers Jez Butterworth and David Glasser apparently helped smooth things over.
      
    
              Mirren also publicly backed Hardy amid the controversy, saying she'd work with him again "in a f***ing heartbeat."
      
    
              Hardy plays Harry Da Souza, a fixer for a powerful London crime family ... and judging by these latest photos, he's not giving up his mob ties anytime soon.

title: Pilot Received Warning Before Mississippi Plane Crash That Killed 6 Family Members
description:
Deadly Mississippi Plane Crash
                          Pilot Received Ominous Warning ...
body:
Deadly Mississippi Plane Crash
                          Pilot Received Ominous Warning ...
                          Before Family of 6 Killed
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                November 26, 2026
                
                            7:56 AM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 26, 2026
                                10:34 AM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              The dad piloting the plane that crashed off the coast of Mississippi, killing him and 5 members of his family, received an ominous warning from air traffic control shortly before the tragedy.
      
    
              An air traffic controller at Gulfport-Biloxi International Airport alerted pilot Brent Stokes to rain and dangerous weather conditions in the area shortly before officials lost contact with the aircraft.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              The family was returning home to Florida from a fishing trip Tuesday when their single-engine Cessna plunged into the waters off Mississippi ... just 2 days before Thanksgiving.
      

              Among those killed were Brent, his son Hunter, his sister Arlyn Knox, her husband Michael Knox, and their 2 sons -- Charles Holden, and Truett.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              As we reported ... crews launched a frantic search after air traffic controllers lost contact with the aircraft. Divers eventually made the heartbreaking discovery ... finding all 6 family members dead inside the wreckage.
      
    
              Federal investigators are working to determine what caused the plane to go down. It's unclear whether the nasty weather played a role in the crash.
